title: Natural Frobenius projection from symmetric invariant tensors
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] of characteristic $p>0$ and $M,N$ arbitrary $k$-vector spaces (that is, modules over $k$, not assumed finite-dimensional). Use module tensor products [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] and extension of scalars [def-weil-module-base-change]. Put $\sigma(a)=a^p$ and $M^{(p)}=M\otimes_{k,\sigma}k$, so $(am)\otimes c=m\otimes a^pc$. Let $I_p(M)=(M^{\otimes p})^{\mathfrak S_p}$ be the subspace fixed by every permutation of the $p$ factors. For any $k$-basis $B$ of $M$, the sums $s_O=\sum_{t\in O}t$ over the distinct tensors in permutation orbits of $B^p$ form a basis of $I_p(M)$. The $k$-linear map $\lambda_M:I_p(M)\to M^{(p)}$ specified by $\lambda_M(b^{\otimes p})=b\otimes1$ and $\lambda_M(s_O)=0$ for every non-singleton orbit is independent of $B$. For every $k$-linear map $h:M\to N$, its tensor power restricts to $I_p(h):I_p(M)\to I_p(N)$ and
$$\lambda_N I_p(h)=h^{(p)}\lambda_M,\qquad h^{(p)}(m\otimes c)=h(m)\otimes c.$$
Let $\tau:M^{\otimes p}\otimes N^{\otimes p}\to(M\otimes N)^{\otimes p}$ interleave factors, and let $\kappa:M^{(p)}\otimes N^{(p)}\to(M\otimes N)^{(p)}$ be the canonical isomorphism with $\kappa((m\otimes a)\otimes(n\otimes b))=(m\otimes n)\otimes ab$. Then for $x\in I_p(M)$ and $y\in I_p(N)$,
$$\lambda_{M\otimes N}(\tau(x\otimes y))=\kappa(\lambda_M(x)\otimes\lambda_N(y)).$$
Here $\tau(x\otimes y)$ is invariant under simultaneous permutations of the paired factors. For $M=k$, the canonical identification $k^{(p)}\to k$, $a\otimes c\mapsto a^pc$, sends $\lambda_k(1^{\otimes p})$ to $1$.

source.place: Section 11(i), diagram preceding Definition 11.39, printed p.224; linear-algebra properties implicit in the diagram, made precise here.

proof.text: Choose bases $B,C$ of $M,N$ using [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-free]. By [lem-sfb-finite-tensor-product-basis-coordinates], the words $B^p$ give a basis of $M^{\otimes p}$, even when $B$ is infinite. Permutations reindex these words, so an invariant vector has coefficients constant on each orbit. Its support is finite, hence it is the finite sum of those constant coefficients times $s_O$. Conversely each $s_O$ is invariant, and a relation among different $s_O$ has every coefficient zero by looking at one word in each disjoint orbit. This proves the asserted orbit basis. A singleton orbit is exactly a constant word: invariance under transpositions makes all entries equal.

source.place: Section 11(i), printed p.224, invariant-tensor arrow before Definition 11.39; agent-written coordinate verification of the linear algebra implicit there.

proof.text: The characteristic $p$ of a field is prime: a factorization $p=rs$ with $1<r,s<p$ would give two nonzero elements $r\cdot1,s\cdot1$ with zero product. For a nonconstant word orbit $O\subset B^p$, choose a letter occurring $r$ times, where $0<r<p$. Count pairs $(w,i)$ with $w\in O$ and that letter in position $i$. The count is $r|O|$. Permuting positions gives bijections between the fibers at any two positions, so it is also $p a$, where $a$ is the number of words having that letter in the first position. Thus $r|O|=pa$ in the integers. Since $p$ is prime and $0<r<p$, Euclid's elementary divisibility property gives $p\mid |O|$. Consequently $|O|\cdot1_k=0$. This argument uses only finite counting and prime divisibility; it does not divide by $p!$ or by an orbit size in $k$.

source.place: Section 11(i), printed p.224, invariant-tensor arrow before Definition 11.39; agent-written coordinate verification of the linear algebra implicit there.

proof.text: The ring map $\sigma$ is supplied by [def-weil-ring-frobenius]. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-free-module-base-change-free] to $k\xrightarrow{\sigma}k$: $(b\otimes1)_{b\in B}$ is a basis of $M^{(p)}$. Using the orbit basis of step 1, define $\lambda_{M,B}$ by the specified images and extend linearly. Equivalently, for invariant $z$ whose word coefficients are $z_w$, it is $\sum_{b\in B}z_{(b,\ldots,b)}(b\otimes1)$, a finite sum. The balancing rule of [def-weil-module-base-change] is $(ab)\otimes c=b\otimes a^pc$. In particular, if $m=\sum_b a_b b$, then $m\otimes1=\sum_b a_b^p(b\otimes1)$.

source.place: Section 11(i), printed p.224, invariant-tensor arrow before Definition 11.39; agent-written coordinate verification of the linear algebra implicit there.

proof.text: Let $h:M\to N$ be linear and write $h(b_i)=\sum_j h_{ji}c_j$. Its tensor power commutes with each permutation, as both composites take $m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_p$ to the same permuted tensor of the $h(m_i)$; these tensors generate by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. It therefore restricts to invariants. For an orbit $O$ with representative $(i_1,\ldots,i_p)$, [lem-sfb-finite-tensor-product-basis-coordinates] gives the coefficient of $c_j^{\otimes p}$ in $h^{\otimes p}(s_O)$ as $|O|\prod_{r=1}^p h_{j,i_r}$: the product is unchanged by permuting the $i_r$. For a nonconstant orbit this is zero by step 2. For the singleton $b_i^{\otimes p}$ it is $h_{ji}^p$. Step 3 now gives $\lambda_{N,C}h^{\otimes p}(b_i^{\otimes p})=\sum_j h_{ji}^p(c_j\otimes1)=h(b_i)\otimes1$. Both sides vanish on every nonconstant orbit sum. These equalities on the orbit basis prove $\lambda_{N,C}I_p(h)=h^{(p)}\lambda_{M,B}$, with $h^{(p)}$ the base-changed map of [def-weil-module-base-change].

source.place: Section 11(i), printed p.224, invariant-tensor arrow before Definition 11.39; agent-written coordinate verification of the linear algebra implicit there.

proof.text: In step 4 take $N=M$ and $h=\mathrm{id}_M$, choosing any second basis $C$ of the same space. Both $I_p(h)$ and $h^{(p)}$ are identity maps, so that equality says $\lambda_{M,C}=\lambda_{M,B}$. Hence $\lambda_M$ is independent of the basis; step 4 is its required naturality. Notice that no spanning claim for the pure powers $m^{\otimes p}$ is needed.

source.place: Section 11(i), printed p.224, invariant-tensor arrow before Definition 11.39; agent-written coordinate verification of the linear algebra implicit there.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-finite-tensor-product-basis-coordinates] for two factors to give $M\otimes N$ the basis $B\times C$, and also to give $M^{(p)}\otimes N^{(p)}$ the basis $(b\otimes1)\otimes(c\otimes1)$. By [lem-weil-pbc-free-module-base-change-free], $(b\otimes c)\otimes1$ is a basis of $(M\otimes N)^{(p)}$. The base-changed bilinear tensor map from [def-weil-module-base-change] therefore induces the isomorphism $\kappa$ sending the first displayed basis to the second. Bilinearity gives exactly the formula with coefficient $ab$ in the statement. The interleaving map $\tau$ is defined on pure tensors by pairing the factors; tensor universality [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product] also constructs its inverse by unpairing. For each permutation $g$, $g\tau(x\otimes y)=\tau(gx\otimes gy)$ by evaluating on pure tensors. Thus $\tau(x\otimes y)$ is invariant when $x,y$ are invariant.

source.place: Section 11(i), printed p.224, invariant-tensor arrow before Definition 11.39; agent-written coordinate verification of the linear algebra implicit there.

proof.text: Write the word coefficients of $x$ and $y$ in the tensor bases from [lem-sfb-finite-tensor-product-basis-coordinates] as $x_{i_1,\ldots,i_p}$ and $y_{j_1,\ldots,j_p}$. The coefficient of the paired word $((i_1,j_1),\ldots,(i_p,j_p))$ in $\tau(x\otimes y)$ is their product, by bilinearity. In particular its constant-word coefficient at $(b,c)$ is $x_{b,\ldots,b}y_{c,\ldots,c}$. The formula of step 3 therefore makes both sides of the requested tensor identity equal to the same finite sum $\sum_{b,c}x_{b,\ldots,b}y_{c,\ldots,c}((b\otimes c)\otimes1)$. Finally take the basis $\{1\}$ of $k$: the definition gives $\lambda_k(1^{\otimes p})=1\otimes1$. The balanced map $a\otimes c\mapsto a^pc$ is inverse to $c\mapsto1\otimes c$, since $a\otimes c=1\otimes a^pc$; it sends that value to $1$.
